clue.text: Daily Mail has no trouble spelling

parts.note: a daily is a British cleaning lady, also called a char

indicators.note: the word mail is left without the letters for the trouble word that follows

parts.note: taken as written, before the trouble is removed
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: A sly dig at a tabloid newspaper whose spelling is apparently effortless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily Mail' poses as the newspaper; in Britain a daily is a cleaner who comes in each day. 'has no' strips the trouble from Mail, leaving just M.
explanation.definitionFit: A spell is a magic charm, so spelling here is a piece of magic or enchantment.

clue.text: About to entertain lavishly, look up place to eat

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means about
to fete someone is to honour them with lavish hospitality

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for look is read from bottom to top

parts.note: an air is a look or manner

explanation.surface: Someone gets ready to host a lavish party and goes off to find a venue.
explanation.walkthrough: The stored clue had a stray 'times'; the page prints no such word. 'up' turns AIR into RIA.
explanation.definitionFit: A cafeteria is a self-service restaurant, somewhere you go for a meal.

clue.text: A carriage overturned by itself

indicators.note: turned upside down in a down clue, so the word for carriage reads upwards

parts.note: a trap is a light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage

explanation.surface: A carriage lies upside down on its own after an accident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturned' turns TRAP into PART.
explanation.definitionFit: Something set apart stands alone, separate from the rest.

clue.text: Second salesman reduced wine

parts.note: mo is short for moment, a second

indicators.note: cut short, so the word for salesman loses its final letter

parts.note: a seller is one who sells

explanation.surface: A salesman knocks down the price of a wine in a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' drops the last letter of SELLER, leaving SELLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Moselle is a white wine from the valley of the river of that name in Germany.

clue.text: Assault with dreadful bludgeon, mostly — awful weapon

parts.note: to do someone is slang for attacking or beating them up

indicators.note: a dreadful mess of letters signals they must be rearranged
most of the word, so bludgeon loses its final letter

explanation.surface: An attack with a nasty club is described as a terrible weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the final letter of the club; 'dreadful' then shuffles what is left. The doodlebug was the V-1 flying bomb that hit London in 1944.
explanation.definitionFit: The doodlebug was the V-1 flying bomb that terrorised London in the Second World War.

clue.text: Produces a rough game, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is what is spoken, so the word for game is taken by its sound

parts.note: draughts is the British name for the board game checkers

explanation.surface: Someone produces a rough-and-tumble game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a rough' is a noun here, a rough version, so 'Produces a rough' works as a verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who drafts writes an early, unpolished version of a document.

clue.text: On holiday, stop delivery

parts.note: someone off is away from work, on leave
a break is a stop or pause

explanation.surface: Someone on holiday cancels their deliveries.
explanation.walkthrough: An off-break is a cricket delivery: a ball spun so it turns into a right-handed batsman from the off side.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a bowler's delivery is a single ball bowled, and the off-break is one kind of spin ball.

clue.text: Does each such charge let one barge through?

definitions.text: Does each such charge let one barge through?

parts.words: Does each such charge let one barge through?
parts.note: read as a canal fee: the toll paid each time a boat passes through a gated stretch of water

explanation.surface: A question about whether a fee lets a barge pass.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a charge in the sense of a rush, letting a barge push through; really it is a canal toll.
explanation.definitionFit: Lockage is the toll paid for passing through the locks of a canal.

clue.text: Elizabeth briefly held up by chap from South America

indicators.note: the name for chap holds the other name inside it

parts.note: Brian is a man's name, standing for any chap

indicators.note: in a down clue this reads the shortened name from bottom to top

parts.note: Liza is a short form of the name Elizabeth

explanation.surface: Elizabeth is delayed for a while by a South American man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held' looks like a passive verb with 'by chap', but it is the container signal, and 'up' reverses the shortened name in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A Brazilian is a person or thing from Brazil, the largest country of South America.

clue.text: Robot providing state with record turnover

indicators.note: turning over the whole run, so both pieces read backwards together

parts.note: ME is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Maine
a log is a written record

explanation.surface: A robot supplies a state with record financial turnover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turnover' reverses MELOG as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: In Jewish folklore a golem is a clay figure brought to life, an artificial man or automaton.

clue.text: Signal to teachers what's required to raise standards

parts.note: to flag is to signal
a school's staff is its teachers

explanation.surface: An instruction to teachers about how to improve school standards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'standards' means flags, not levels of attainment.
explanation.definitionFit: A flagstaff is the pole on which a flag, or standard, is hoisted.

clue.text: Stroke fawn

definitions.meaning: a swimming style done face down with alternate overarm movements
to grovel or toady to someone

explanation.definitionFit: The front swimming stroke and abject grovelling share this word, as in to creep before a superior.

clue.text: To a militarist, an ordered form of government?

indicators.note: put into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: To a soldier, an orderly system of rule might be what he wants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' rearranges TOAMILITARISTAN; a militarist would like an ordered state.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a centralised, dictatorial system of rule demanding complete subservience to the state.

clue.text: Put ingredient for salad dressing down

definitions.meaning: a peppery leaf also called arugula
British informal for a severe reprimand

explanation.surface: Someone adds an item to a salad dressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put' is a link word; 'dressing' is not salad dressing but part of 'dressing down', a telling-off.
explanation.definitionFit: The salad leaf arugula and a stern telling-off (to get a rocket) share this British word.

clue.text: Tom, for example, is put on one list, say, or another

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
a means one

indicators.note: say means spoken aloud, so the sound of the list word is spelt differently

parts.note: a log is a list or record of events

explanation.surface: A tomcat is entered on one list or another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' is the definition: another list, after the 'list' of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A catalogue is a further list, a systematic register of items.

clue.text: Medicinal plant needed for emperor

definitions.meaning: a herb whose root is used as a sedative
a Roman ruler of the third century AD

explanation.surface: A herbal remedy is required for an emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: The sedative herb and the third-century Roman ruler captured by the Persians share the name.

clue.text: Endlessly kind friend? Of course!

indicators.note: without its end, so the word for kind loses its last letter

parts.note: nature means kind or sort, as in things of that nature
an ally is a friend

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that an endlessly kind friend is, of course, wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' trims NATURE to NATUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturally is an exclamation of agreement meaning certainly, as expected.

clue.text: Statesman from the period of various kings

definitions.meaning: read literally, a man from a state, here the US state or the Caucasian country

definitions.text: from the period of various kings
definitions.meaning: the era when the four Hanoverian kings named George reigned, 1714-1830

explanation.surface: A politician from the reign of several monarchs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Statesman' is not a politician but a man from a state: someone from Georgia.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Georgia, and the style or era of the four British Kings George, share this word.

clue.text: Anthea's constituents

parts.note: the name Anthea breaks into the little words a, an, the and a, grammatical parts of speech

explanation.surface: The voters of an MP named Anthea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'constituents' suggests voters, but means the parts that make up the name: A, AN, THE, A.
explanation.definitionFit: A, an and the are the English grammatical articles, and they compose the name.

clue.text: Reacted after heart transplant — made a fuss

indicators.note: the central letter of the word reacted is taken out and transplanted elsewhere

explanation.surface: A patient responded after a heart transplant by creating a scene.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart of REACTED is C, its middle letter; moved to the front it gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To create, in British informal use, is to make a fuss or complain noisily.

clue.text: Without piano at home, arrange for another instrument

indicators.note: in its old sense of outside, so one word goes around the others

parts.note: to set is to arrange, as in set a table
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
in means at home

explanation.surface: With no piano in the house, someone arranges to get a different instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like it means lacking, but here it carries its old sense of outside, so it signals a container.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinet is a small harpsichord, a different keyboard instrument from the piano.

clue.text: Put out tip here, please, in the traditional way

indicators.note: put out of place, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a tip to be left here, in an old-fashioned way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' rearranges TIPHERE.
explanation.definitionFit: Prithee is an archaic contraction of I pray thee, an old way of saying please.

clue.text: Upstart-placed in a dock in court

indicators.note: put inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: to dock is to trim or cut short
the start of up is its first letter, U

explanation.surface: An upstart is put in the dock at a court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upstart' reads as start of 'Up', giving U, placed in A TRIM.
explanation.definitionFit: An atrium is a central courtyard or open hall inside a building.

clue.text: Appropriate type of dog for Jason?

definitions.text: Appropriate type of dog for Jason?

parts.words: Appropriate type of dog for Jason?
parts.note: read as a breed named for the Greek hero who brought back the Golden Fleece

explanation.surface: What sort of dog would suit someone called Jason?
explanation.walkthrough: Jason of the Argonauts fetched the Golden Fleece, so a dog breed named for golden fetching suits him.
explanation.definitionFit: This breed of gun dog is named for its golden coat and for fetching shot game.

clue.text: Arranged rose

definitions.meaning: stood or got out of bed

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both dressed or presented and got out of bed.

clue.text: Boast about shape of neck to relative

parts.note: a V-neck is a common neckline shape
an aunt is a relative

explanation.surface: Someone boasts to a relative about the shape of their neck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is a link here, not a container or reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: To vaunt is to brag about something.

clue.text: Nothing odd in string that is fully stretched

indicators.note: take no odd-placed letters, so only the second, fourth and so on of the words string and that are kept

explanation.surface: A string with nothing strange about it, pulled taut.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the odd letters of STRING THAT leaves the even ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tight is taut, pulled as far as it will go.

clue.text: Pats farm animal? That's a silly thing to say

parts.note: Pat is a traditional nickname for an Irishman
a bull is a farm animal

explanation.surface: A farm animal belonging to someone called Pat, followed by a dismissive remark.
explanation.walkthrough: An Irish bull is a ludicrous self-contradictory statement, such as 'if you don't receive this letter, write and tell me'.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase names a self-contradictory or ludicrous remark, a comic verbal blunder.

clue.text: Sapper, for example, reconstructed mounds? Yep!

indicators.note: built again in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A military engineer rebuilds earthworks and cheerfully agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: Sapper was the pen name of H. C. McNeile, author of the Bulldog Drummond novels; a sapper is also an army engineer, hence the mounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapper is a pen name, the made-up name under which a writer publishes.

clue.text: Start off some top people as competitors

indicators.note: the start of the word is taken off, removing its first letter

parts.note: the gentry are people of high social rank

explanation.surface: Some top people begin by signing up as competitors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start off' removes the G of GENTRY.
explanation.definitionFit: The entry for a race or contest is the full list of those taking part.
